data: Motherhood Family and Childcare in India

The aim of this course is to interrogate the sociocultural constitution of motherhood as a psychological experience. Challenging the Eurocentric depiction of the mother-infant dyad reproduced in psychology literature, this course approaches a sensemaking process through the intersectionality of cultural psychology, feminist intersectionality, and critical developmental psychology perspectives. Through the course, students will examine motherhood as a social institution and study the nurturing bonds women have with children and others. In so doing, students will focus on analyzing the stereotypical representations of the mothers as “monstrous” and “consecrated”. Subsequently, students will have the opportunity to examine the developmental experiences of women such as pregnancy, childbirth, and caregiving rooted in the family and communal life in India. Students will have the opportunity to understand how family life, cultural practices, technologies, and structural inequities structure multiple trajectories for motherhood and their childcare decisions.  Lastly, taking Burman’s “Child as Method” as an analytic and pedagogical device, students will unpack various contemporary and historical discourses on childhood and parenting shapes and regulates motherhood as a site for “oppression” and “resistance”. We will explore how everyday acts of mothering are performed as resistance to prevailing sociocultural norms.
